entries.title: The genealogies and Ussher
entries.summary: Add up the ages in Genesis 5 and 11 and you get a date for Adam. Ussher did. Does the text intend it?
entries.plain: The real question: can you add up the ages in the genealogies to get the age of humanity? **Some family trees list every generation. Some jump to the one that matters.** You cannot always tell which kind you are holding from a single line. Only the first kind can be added up, and the question is which kind Genesis 5 and 11 are.
entries.q: Archbishop Ussher's famous date for creation came from two moves: a single literal week, and the genealogies treated as an unbroken father-to-son chain with no gaps. The second move can be checked against how the Bible's own genealogies work.
entries.heb: The formula is "A fathered B, and after fathering B lived x years." Kenneth Kitchen, quoted by Lennox, shows that such lists can record actual fatherhood or condense a longer series: in Matthew 1:8 Jehoram is called the father of Uzziah, which skips three generations. The pre-flood life spans run to the 900s.
entries.len: Lennox follows Kitchen: on the internal evidence of Scripture the age of humanity is indeterminate, though whether it stretches far enough to fit current estimates is another matter. He keeps four ages distinct, the universe, the earth, life and humanity, and says the supernatural character of human creation matters more than its date.
entries.lenSrc: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World, ch. 4, The Antiquity of Humanity
entries.wal: In the IVP Bible Background Commentary, Walton and his co-authors say there is no satisfactory explanation of the long pre-flood life spans. They note that the Sumerian King List gives pre-flood reigns as long as 43,200 years, and that converted from the Sumerian base-sixty system to decimal, the numbers fall in the range of the Genesis ages. They also note that Enoch, seventh in the line and taken by God, parallels the seventh pre-flood sage Utuabzu, who ascended to heaven. Separately, Walton argues the presence of Adam in genealogies shows the authors treated him as a historical person, since ancient genealogies list real people.
entries.walSrc: Walton, Matthews and Chavalas, IVP Bible Background Commentary: Old Testament, on Genesis 5; Walton, The Lost World of Adam and Eve, proposition 11
entries.others: The MacArthur Study Bible reads the ages as literal years and attributes them to a pre-flood water canopy that filtered ultraviolet light, and puts creation no earlier than about 10,000 years ago.
entries.cost: The gap reading has to explain why Genesis gives the father's age at the son's birth, which looks designed for counting. The literal reading has to explain the skipping that other biblical genealogies plainly do. The Sumerian King List comparison carries its own cost and should not be leaned on: it assumes a base-sixty count was carried into a base-ten text, while the same commentary notes the Hebrews used base ten as far back as writing goes, and the converted numbers only land in the general range of the Genesis ages. They do not match name for name or figure for figure. The MacArthur explanation of the long lives, a pre-flood water canopy filtering ultraviolet light, is likewise a scientific proposal the text does not state.
entries.not: **Not a dismissal of the genealogies.** Walton uses them to argue for a historical Adam, and Lennox takes the people in them as real.
sources: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World (2021), ch. 4, with K. A. Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament (Eerdmans, 2003), as quoted there
Walton, Matthews and Chavalas, IVP Bible Background Commentary: Old Testament (IVP, 2000), on Genesis 5:3-32 and 5:21-24

entries.title: The flood and its extent
entries.summary: The whole earth, all flesh, every high mountain. Global, or the whole known world?
entries.plain: The real question: was Noah's flood worldwide, or did it cover the world Noah's readers knew? **It rained everywhere this weekend.** From the state weather desk, that means the state. Said of the planet, it means the planet. Everywhere and all take their range from the speaker's frame, and the question is whose frame the flood narrative uses.
entries.q: The flood narrative uses universal-sounding phrases again and again. Whether they mean the planet or the known world is the question, and it bears on how the Nephilim reappear after the flood in Numbers 13:33.
entries.heb: The phrase "the whole earth," kol erets, appears in passages that are plainly local (Heiser lists Genesis 13:9 and 41:57 among others, where the frame is a region). "All humankind," kol adam, also appears where it cannot mean every person on the planet. Genesis 10 lists the nations descended from Noah's sons, and all of them sit in the ancient Near East, the Mediterranean and the Aegean.
entries.kjv: And the waters prevailed exceedingly upon the earth; and all the high hills, that were under the whole heaven, were covered.
entries.kjvRole: "high hills" where the ESV has "high mountains"
entries.kjvNote: The King James reads "all the high hills" and the ESV "all the high mountains." The MacArthur Study Bible builds part of its global argument on the mountains. Either way the verse adds "under the whole heaven," which is the phrase the extent argument turns on.
entries.len: Lennox does not take up the extent of the flood in Seven Days. His concern is creation and the days. He treats Genesis 1 to 11 as describing actual events, including the flood through which Noah and his family were preserved.
entries.lenSrc: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World, ch. 3
entries.wal: In the IVP Bible Background Commentary, Walton and his co-authors set out the Atrahasis and Gilgamesh flood accounts and say there is no reason to doubt that they and Genesis refer to the same flood. The similarities come from a shared event, the differences from each culture viewing it through its own theology. The commentary reads "windows of heaven" as observer's language, not scientific description.
entries.walSrc: Walton, Matthews and Chavalas, IVP Bible Background Commentary: Old Testament, on Genesis 7-8 and the sidebar on ancient Near Eastern flood accounts
entries.others: Heiser sets out the textual case for a regional flood: kol erets and kol adam in local contexts, the Table of Nations confined to the known world, and Psalm 104:9, which he reads as God promising never to cover the earth with water as at creation. He offers it as one of two ways to explain giants after the flood. The MacArthur Study Bible argues the opposite: "under the whole heaven" and waters above the highest mountains prove a global flood, and more than 270 flood stories worldwide trace to it.
entries.cost: The regional reading has to account for the repeated universal language and for 7:19-20. The global reading has to explain the local use of the same phrases elsewhere and the Nephilim of Numbers 13:33, who appear after a flood that, on that reading, left no one but Noah's family. Two supports on either side are weaker than they look. Psalm 104:9 does not mention the flood; reading it as ruling one out is Heiser's inference from its creation setting. The MacArthur note's figure of more than 270 flood stories worldwide is given without a source.
entries.not: **Not the same as denying the flood happened.** Every source here treats it as a real event.
sources: Heiser, Reversing Hermon (2017), ch. 1, Nephilim after the Flood, and nn. 38-39
Walton, Matthews and Chavalas, IVP Bible Background Commentary: Old Testament (2000), on Genesis 7:11-8:12 and Ancient Near Eastern Flood Accounts

entries.title: The sons of God and the daughters of men
entries.summary: Genesis 6:1-4 is the strangest passage in Genesis 1 to 11. The Divine Council Index has the full treatment; this is how it sits in the primeval history.
entries.plain: The real question: who were the "sons of God" in Genesis 6, and why does the story sit right before the flood? **"Sons of the prophets" were not the prophets' children.** Hebrew uses "son of" for belonging to a group. So "sons of God" could mean divine beings, godly men or kings who claimed divine descent.
entries.q: Four verses introduce the sons of God, the daughters of men, a limit of 120 years and the Nephilim, and then the narrative moves straight into the flood. How they connect decides how much of the flood story is about human sin alone.
entries.heb: The phrase is bene ha-elohim, the same phrase used of heavenly beings in Job 1:6 and 38:7. The Nephilim are said to be on the earth "in those days, and also afterward."
entries.len: Lennox does not address Genesis 6:1-4 in Seven Days.
entries.lenSrc: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World
entries.wal: The IVP Bible Background Commentary notes that sons of God refers to angels elsewhere, but that ancient kings were often thought to be engendered by deity, and reads the offense in light of the Gilgamesh Epic's royal abuse of the wedding night. Walton's fuller case for the royal reading, and his three objections to the divine reading, are summarized in the Divine Council Index.
entries.walSrc: Walton, Matthews and Chavalas, IVP Bible Background Commentary: Old Testament, on Genesis 6:2-3
entries.others: Heiser reads the sons of God as divine beings, with 1 Enoch preserving the original Mesopotamian backstory. The MacArthur Study Bible also reads them as fallen angels, who it says possessed human male bodies. It reports and rejects two other views: that the sons of God were the line of Seth marrying the daughters of Cain, and that they were human kings building harems.
entries.cost: See the Divine Council Index entry for what each reading still leaves open.
entries.not: **Not a side story.** Its placement before the flood is part of why the passage matters.

entries.title: Babel
entries.summary: One language, a tower with its top in the heavens, and the scattering of the nations. The tower is a Mesopotamian building with a Mesopotamian purpose.
entries.plain: The real question: what were they building at Babel, and why did it matter to God? **The town put up a tower you could see from three counties.** It might have been about pride, worship, defense, or a way to keep everyone together. The building tells you what they made. The text tells you what God thought of it.
entries.q: The story is short and the tower gets more attention than the verses give it. What was it, and what does the scattering do?
entries.heb: The account is set in Shinar, the lower Tigris-Euphrates basin, linguistically equivalent to Sumer. The builders use baked brick and bitumen, the technology of southern Mesopotamia, where stone had to be hauled from far away.
entries.len: Lennox does not address Babel in Seven Days. In appendix A he cites Kitchen that the theme of the division of languages is very old, recorded in a Sumerian composition about a king of around 2600 BC, as evidence for the early date of the material.
entries.lenSrc: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World, appendix A
entries.wal: The IVP Bible Background Commentary connects the account with Sumerian urbanization and ziggurat building, notes a Sumerian epic, Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta, that remembers a time when all spoke to Enlil in one tongue, and reads the brick technology as authentically Mesopotamian.
entries.walSrc: Walton, Matthews and Chavalas, IVP Bible Background Commentary: Old Testament, on Genesis 11:1-9
entries.others: Heiser reads Babel as the event behind Deuteronomy 32:8-9, where God divided the nations and allotted them to the sons of God, which begins the cosmic geography of the rest of the Bible. The MacArthur Study Bible reads it as an act of pride led by Nimrod.
entries.cost: The background reading explains the building. It does not by itself say why God's response was to divide languages and nations. The council reading needs Deuteronomy 32:8 in its Dead Sea Scrolls form, the most contested text in the Divine Council Index.
entries.not: **Not settled by the building.** The ziggurat as a staircase for a god to come down is the background reading the IVP commentary gives for the tower. The MacArthur Study Bible reads the same tower as a monument to pride. The brick and bitumen fit both.

entries.title: Enuma Elish and Genesis 1
entries.summary: A Babylonian creation epic on seven tablets, with humans made on the sixth. Borrowing, a shared world, or a reply?
entries.plain: The real question: did Genesis copy older Babylonian creation stories? **Two families tell the story of how the town was founded.** Some details match. One borrowed from the other, both remember the same thing, or one is answering the other. Comparing Genesis with its neighbours shows how much they share and where they part.
entries.q: Since the nineteenth century the parallels between Genesis 1 and the Babylonian epic Enuma Elish have been used to argue that Genesis is derived from it. The parallels are real. What they prove is the question.
entries.heb: The Hebrew tehom, the deep, is related to Tiamat, the goddess Marduk splits to make heaven and earth. Kitchen, quoted by Lennox, points out that the word also exists in Ugaritic and means simply deep or abyss. Genesis 1 does not use the ordinary names for the sun and moon.
entries.len: Lennox grants the surface similarities: seven tablets and seven days, a similar order, humans on the sixth tablet and sixth day. Then he lists the differences: no theogony, no warring gods, nothing made out of a god's body, no deified sun or stars, and humans as the image of God rather than slaves to ease the gods' labour. He follows Kitchen that in the ancient world simple accounts grow into elaborate legends, not the reverse, and that there is no proven link between the two texts.
entries.lenSrc: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World, appendix A, with Kitchen and Millard as quoted there
entries.wal: Walton uses the ancient texts to recover what an ancient reader assumed, not to derive Genesis from them. In Genesis 1 as Ancient Cosmology he calls many attempts to trace literary trails from ancient Near Eastern texts to Genesis too facile, more like a Rorschach test than clear literary links, and turns instead to the shared cognitive environment. In Enuma Elish, Marduk's creating is followed by building a temple where the gods find rest, which he reads as the same cluster of creation, temple, rest and rule that Genesis 1 ends on. He also points out where Genesis differs: in the Bible, God has no needs and orders the cosmos around people, not around the gods.
entries.walSrc: Walton, Genesis 1 as Ancient Cosmology, introduction; The Lost World of Genesis One, propositions 2, 4 and 7
entries.others: The de-deification theory, which Lennox reports and rejects with Kitchen and Millard, holds that Israel took a mythological text and stripped the gods out of it during the exile.
entries.cost: Lennox's emphasis on difference has to make room for the shared features Walton finds meaningful, such as the temple and rest. Walton's use of the parallels has to keep them as background without letting them set the meaning.
entries.not: **Not a copy.** Neither pole thinks Genesis was copied from Enuma Elish, and Kitchen's verdict, as Lennox quotes it, is that the attempts to prove a direct relationship have had to be abandoned.
sources: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World (2021), appendix A, quoting Enuma Elish and K. A. Kitchen and A. R. Millard
Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One (2009), propositions 2, 4, 7
Walton, Genesis 1 as Ancient Cosmology (Eisenbrauns, 2011), introduction

entries.title: Genesis 1 never says sun
entries.summary: Day four has the greater light and the lesser light. The ordinary Hebrew words for sun and moon are not used. On that fact, every reading agrees.
entries.plain: The real question: why does Genesis 1 call the sun and moon "the greater light" and "the lesser light"? **Call the boss "the guy with the bigger desk."** Everyone still knows who you mean, but the title is gone. That the names are missing is a fact anyone can check. What it was meant to say is where readers differ.
entries.q: Readers notice the roundabout phrasing in 1:16 and wonder whether it means anything. The fact itself is not in dispute. The text uses lights, the greater light and the lesser light, and never the ordinary words.
entries.heb: Lennox notes, with Kitchen and others, that the usual names of the sun and moon are not used in Genesis 1. The lights are given jobs: to separate day from night, to serve as signs for seasons, days and years, and to give light on the earth.
entries.len: Lennox reads the omission as part of Genesis 1's protest against idolatry. In Egypt the sun god Ra was chief god, his name embedded in the title Pharaoh. Paul Marston, quoted by Lennox, imagines the shock of finding that Ra was a mere lamp created on day four. Leon Kass goes further: the sun is the common feature of every incongruity in the chapter, and its demotion is deliberate.
entries.lenSrc: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World, ch. 3 and appendix A
entries.wal: Walton reads day four as installing functionaries. The text offers no indication of the material nature of the celestial bodies. All it says of them is where they are placed and what they are for: signs, seasons, days and years.
entries.walSrc: Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One, proposition 6
entries.cost: The fact is settled. What it was for is a separate question: a polemic against sun worship (Lennox, Kass, Marston), or simply the functional focus of the whole chapter (Walton). The two answers fit together.
entries.not: **Not a claim that the sun is unimportant.** The lights rule the day and the night. They are demoted from gods, not from their work.
sources: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World (2021), ch. 3, quoting Paul Marston and Leon Kass, and appendix A
Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One (2009), proposition 6

entries.title: Does Genesis rule on evolution?
entries.summary: Lennox reads two "and God said" moments as lines no unguided process crosses. Walton reads the text as making no material claim at all.
entries.plain: The real question: does Genesis 1 say anything about how living things came to be, or only that God did it? **The recipe says: add eggs.** It does not tell you which hen laid them. Lennox thinks the recipe still marks the steps that cannot happen on their own. Walton thinks it is not a recipe.
entries.q: The question is not whether God created. Both poles say he did. It is whether the text draws lines that rule out particular mechanisms.
entries.heb: Day three has two "And God said" statements: one for dry land and seas, one for vegetation. Day six has two: one for land animals, one for humans. The earth "brings forth" vegetation and living creatures at God's command.
entries.len: Lennox sees the double "And God said" on days three and six as deliberate: you do not get from non-life to life, or from animals to humans, without a word from God. Genesis affirms that life has a material, chemical substrate (let the earth bring forth) but denies that it is nothing but chemistry. He thinks human evolution from earlier hominids does not fit Genesis 2, especially the making of the woman. His appendix D engages theistic evolution at length.
entries.lenSrc: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World, ch. 3, ch. 4 and appendix D
entries.wal: Walton argues that since Genesis makes no claim about material mechanisms, it does not offer a competing claim to the scientific account of human origins. That does not mean the science is right, only that the Bible's claim is that whatever happened, God did it. He holds that humans could be viewed as distinct creatures and a special creation of God even if there was material continuity.
entries.walSrc: Walton, The Lost World of Adam and Eve, propositions 8 and 21
entries.others: Evolutionary creation, represented in Lennox's discussion by Denis Alexander, accepts common descent and places Adam and Eve as historical figures chosen within an existing population.
entries.cost: Lennox has to show that the double fiat marks a discontinuity in mechanism, not just in importance. Walton has to persuade readers that a God-is-responsible claim with no mechanism is what the original audience heard.
entries.not: **Not a debate between faith and science.** Lennox is a scientist arguing from the text; Walton is a text scholar arguing the text makes no scientific claim.
sources: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World (2021), chs. 3-4 and appendix D
Walton, The Lost World of Adam and Eve (2015), propositions 8 and 21

entries.title: John Walton
entries.summary: Wheaton Old Testament scholar. Genesis 1 is ancient cosmology about functional origins, the inauguration of the cosmos as God's temple.
entries.plain: Walton's big idea in one line: Genesis 1 is the story of the world being set up to work, with God moving in, not the story of the world's raw materials being made. **The house was built years ago. Tonight the family moves in.** That is what he thinks the seven days describe.
entries.q: What Walton holds, in his own terms, stated at full strength.
entries.wal: Genesis 1 is ancient cosmology and makes no claims about modern science. The ancient world defined existence by function. Bara concerns functions. The starting state is nonfunctional, not shapeless. Days one to three establish functions, days four to six install functionaries. Divine rest is in a temple and the cosmos is a temple. The seven days are literal days of the inauguration of that temple and do not concern material origins. So there is no biblical position on the age of the earth. Adam and Eve are real people in a real past, and the forming accounts are archetypal statements about every human.
entries.walSrc: Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One, propositions 1-18; The Lost World of Adam and Eve, propositions 1-21
entries.cost: Critics, including those Lennox cites, ask whether one ancient ontology can be applied across the whole Near East, whether a functional emphasis excludes material interest, and whether the temple reading puts more into Genesis 1 than an ancient reader would have found.
entries.not: **Not a denial that God made matter.** Walton says so repeatedly.
sources: Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One (IVP Academic, 2009)
Walton, The Lost World of Adam and Eve (IVP Academic, 2015)
Walton, Genesis 1 as Ancient Cosmology (Eisenbrauns, 2011)

entries.title: John Lennox
entries.summary: Oxford mathematician and philosopher of science. The days are open to several readings; the text leaves the age of the universe open; God's word marks the decisive steps.
entries.plain: Lennox's big idea in one line: the Bible could be read as saying the earth is young, but it does not have to be, the same way it once seemed to say the earth does not move. **The Bible says the earth is fixed on pillars.** Nobody now reads that as astronomy. He thinks the age of the earth is the same kind of question.
entries.q: What Lennox holds, in his own terms, stated at full strength.
entries.len: Genesis 1 to 11 describes real events. The Galileo controversy shows Christians can change their reading of a text without compromising its authority when the evidence is strong. Genesis 1:1 can precede day one, leaving the age of the universe open. Yom has several literal meanings in Genesis 1-2. He does not insist on one reading of the days, favouring a combination of sequence and framework, with sympathy for Gooding's creation days separated by long periods. God's speaking on each day is more important than each day's length. The double "And God said" on days three and six marks the origin of life and of humans. Romans 5:12 concerns human death. Humans are a special creation.
entries.lenSrc: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World, chs. 1-5 and appendices
entries.cost: Lennox admits he does not settle day four and has not solved animal suffering. His "why not both" toward Walton keeps the material reading without fully answering Walton's case that the material reading must be demonstrated.
entries.not: **Not a concordist in the strong sense.** He does not claim Genesis teaches modern science, only that it is consistent with it.
sources: Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World: The Beginning According to Genesis and Science, 10th anniversary ed. (Zondervan Reflective, 2021)

entries.title: Young-earth creationism at its strongest
entries.summary: Six consecutive 24-hour days, a recent creation, a global flood, and no death before the fall. Stated by its own advocates.
entries.plain: The young-earth view in one line: read Genesis the way it sounds, as a week, and let science answer to the text rather than the other way round. **If someone tells you he built a deck in six days, you assume he means six days.** That is the instinct this position defends.
entries.q: The position stated by those who hold it, not by its critics.
entries.others: As set out in the MacArthur Study Bible: creation was recent, out of nothing, and in six consecutive 24-hour days marked by evening and morning. Day with a number in Hebrew always refers to a 24-hour period, and Exodus 20:8-11 confirms the week. Scripture does not support a creation date earlier than about 10,000 years ago. The pre-flood ages are literal years. The flood was global, covering the highest mountains. Satan, a fallen archangel, possessed the serpent.
entries.cost: Two young-earth authors, Paul Nelson and John Mark Reynolds, quoted by Lennox, say they defend a very natural biblical account at the cost of a very plausible scientific picture, and that over the long term this is not a tenable position. Walton grants this position its reading of yom and faults its reading of bara and asah. Lennox grants that Genesis can be read this way and argues it does not have to be. Both point to the need for alternative science, light created in transit, appearance of age, flood geology, to hold the position together.
entries.not: **Not anti-intellectual by definition.** Lennox praises the honesty of young-earth writers who concede the scientific difficulty openly.
sources: The MacArthur Study Bible (ESV), ed. John MacArthur (Crossway, 2010), notes on Genesis 1:1, 1:5, 3:1, 5:5, 7:19-20

Lennox, Seven Days that Divide the World (2021), ch. 3 and n. 77, quoting Paul Nelson and John Mark Reynolds, "Young Earth Creationism," in Three Views on Creation and Evolution, ed. J. P. Moreland and John Mark Reynolds (Zondervan, 1999), 73
Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One (2009), proposition 12

entries.title: Michael Heiser
entries.summary: Reads Genesis 1 to 11 through the divine council: the plural of 1:26, the serpent as a divine rebel, the sons of God, Babel and the nations.
entries.plain: Heiser's big idea in one line: Genesis 1 to 11 has a heavenly household in it as well as a human one, and three rebellions, not one, set up the rest of the Bible. **A family business has two branches.** Trouble in one spills into the other. Heiser reads the early chapters of Genesis that way.
entries.q: Heiser is not one of this tool's poles, because his subject is the unseen realm, not the age of the earth or the mechanics of creation. His reading still touches five entries here.
entries.others: Genesis 1:26 is God addressing his council, with 1:27 recording that God alone created. The image is a status: humans are God's imagers on earth. The serpent is a divine being. Genesis 6:1-4 describes divine beings and the origin of the Nephilim, a reading 1 Enoch preserves. The flood may have been regional, which would explain giants after it. Babel is the moment God allotted the nations to the sons of God, the background to Deuteronomy 32:8-9.
entries.cost: The full costs of each of these readings are set out in the Divine Council Index entries.
entries.not: **Not a third position on the days.** Heiser's reading is compatible with more than one view of the days and does not depend on any of them.
sources: Heiser, The Unseen Realm (Lexham, 2015)
Heiser, Reversing Hermon (2017)
